_about: Each entry puts one known bug back into internal/web and the suite must fail. The set is weighted toward the security decisions rather than the plumbing: a mutant that survives on the CSRF layer or the certificate store means the test suite does not actually pin the control it claims to. Run: python3 scripts/mutate.py scripts/mutations/web.json

mutants.note: the rotation window is gone, so a certificate is served until the day it expires
an expired certificate is served again instead of replaced
a usable certificate on disk is never reused, so every restart re-mints and the pinned fingerprint changes

mutants.old: if err := writeFilePrivate(keyPath, pem.EncodeToMemory(&pem.Block{Type: "EC PRIVATE KEY", Bytes: keyDER}), 0o600); err != nil {
mutants.new: if err := writeFilePrivate(keyPath, pem.EncodeToMemory(&pem.Block{Type: "EC PRIVATE KEY", Bytes: keyDER}), 0o644); err != nil {
mutants.note: the private key is written world-readable
the certificate lasts a day, so the parent re-trusts it every fortnight
a hostname that is not a legal DNS label goes into the SANs, and Safari rejects the whole certificate for it
link-local addresses go into the SANs

mutants.new: if err := func() error { return nil }(); err != nil {
mutants.note: the temp file keeps CreateTemp's 0600-or-umask mode, so the requested mode is never applied
tls: custom accepts an expired certificate at startup and fails on the first handshake instead
one empty path out of two is accepted, so the daemon starts and cannot serve
a private key is stored in a directory anybody can read
the directory is opened following symlinks and able to block
Secure is set on a plain-HTTP listener, so the browser discards the cookie and login loops forever
the session cookie crosses a TLS connection in a form any network observer can replay
Lax still sends the cookie on a top-level cross-site navigation
a CSRF token outlives the session it belongs to
the CSRF token is taken from the session token itself, so anything that can echo the cookie can authorise a POST
logout does not expire the cookie, so a browser keeps presenting a revoked session
the throttle never refuses, so every attempt reaches PBKDF2
a failed login is not counted, so the bucket never fills
the IPv6 zone stays in the key, so one host gets a bucket per interface
a machine with no credential answers "wrong password", sending the operator looking in the wrong place
the wrong-credential branch stops counting failures
the login POST is CSRF-gated, so nobody can ever sign in
a GET is required to carry a CSRF token, which no browser can do

the CSRF comparison leaks timing on a secret. The mutant adds `got == want ||` in front of the constant-time compare. The two
expressions return the same bool for every possible pair of inputs, so no test can
distinguish them: the only difference is how long the comparison takes, and timing
is not an observable a unit test in this package has.

Marking it equivalent is a claim, so it is checkable: delete the `got == want ||`
prefix and every test in internal/web still passes -- in particular
TestAPostWithoutACSRFTokenIsRefusedAndDoesNothing,
TestAPostWithTheSessionsTokenIsAccepted and
TestAnotherSessionsCSRFTokenIsNotAccepted, which together pin that a correct token
is accepted, a missing one is refused, and another session's token is refused. All
three go through this comparison, so they pin that it exists and is reached; none of
them can pin that it is constant-time.

What the mutant is really guarding against -- someone swapping the constant-time
compare for a plain == -- is therefore a review property, not a test property.
the login form can be framed by a hostile page
a dynamic page is cacheable, so who is locked out stays readable after logout
the panic text reaches the client, mapping the binary for anybody on the LAN
a panic is turned into a 500 and never logged, so nobody knows it happened
a JSON client following a redirect gets an HTML login page where it expected a status code
a refused CSRF check leaves no trace
the transport accepts anything a client offers
a content-addressed asset is re-fetched on every page view
an unknown hash falls back to the literal name, so the immutable header can pin a stale file forever
the auth gate lets an anonymous request through

mutants.old: return nil, fmt.Errorf("web: unknown tls mode %q (expected auto, off or custom)", s.TLSMode)
mutants.note: an unknown tls mode falls through to a transport instead of refusing to start

mutants.new: if err := httpSrv.Shutdown(drain); err != nil && false {
mutants.note: in-flight requests are cut off instead of drained
the asset URL hashes the filename, so a content change keeps the same URL and the immutable header pins the old bytes
Serve stops terminating TLS, so a daemon configured `auto` answers plain HTTP on a port it logs as https:// and the Secure cookie can never be set
a broken asset bundle is swallowed, so every /static/ request 404s and the operator gets the unstyled page with nothing in the log
the disabled-transport warning ignores Options.Warn and goes to stdout, the stream an operator redirects away
an injected asset bundle is dropped, so Options.Static does nothing and the constructor's asset check is unreachable again
the bind signal is never sent, so every caller of WaitReady blocks until its own deadline -- the dead field's contract, broken in the other direction
the waiter is released but never told what happened, so a failed bind reports success and the caller reads an empty Addr() with no error to explain it
a Server assembled as a struct literal gets a nil channel, and closing it panics in Serve -- the zero-value rule this package's own tests depend on
a caller that gave up is told the server is ready, so a daemon that never bound looks healthy to the thing supervising it

the enforcement loop dropped from the daemon's runners: the admin UI is served, the dashboard looks healthy, and nobody is ever locked out. This is the exact regression the branch's own 'not wired into this build' notice existed to catch, and a notice is not a test

the empty-chain guard weakened to a nil check, which platform.New can never satisfy -- it always returns a Chain and reports unbuildable backends as an error alongside it. The daemon then starts with zero backends and enforces nothing

the audit pre-flight removed: the writer opens lazily, so an unwritable trail surfaces as the first dropped event hours later instead of as a startup failure the operator who can fix it is standing in front of
